claims.text: Mechanical alloying is an available synthesis method for refractory high-entropy alloys.
Mechanical alloying followed by hot isostatic pressing can produce large-scale RHEA-Cu composite structures.
The mechanically alloyed and HIP-consolidated RHEA-Cu composite will have a stable microstructure despite the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
The feedstock consists of RHEA and Cu powders in near-equiatomic or otherwise tailored compositions.
An inert atmosphere and controlled HIP temperature, pressure, and duration ensure thorough mixing and dense consolidation.
Mechanical alloying produces a fine, homogeneously mixed RHEA-Cu powder feedstock.
HIP consolidates the mixed powder feedstock into near-net-shape bulk material.
Powder-based processing overcomes enthalpy-driven phase separation in RHEA-Cu composites.
Uniform mixing at the powder stage and control of reaction kinetics during consolidation stabilize the composite microstructure.
The proposed process will yield a dense, near-net-shape RHEA-Cu composite.
The resulting RHEA-Cu composite will exhibit limited interfacial reactions and a stable, homogeneous microstructure.
The resulting RHEA-Cu composite will be suitable for high-temperature nuclear reactor applications.
Conventional casting or infiltration often causes incomplete mixing and excessive interfacial reaction zones in RHEA-Cu composites.
Incomplete mixing and excessive interfacial reaction zones lead to non-uniform or unstable microstructures.
Powder composition, milling parameters, and HIP temperature-pressure profiles must be tailored to prevent defects or undesirable intermetallic formation.
Long-term stability and performance of HIP-consolidated RHEA-Cu composites under irradiation and thermal extremes have not been fully verified.
